title: Challenges in Machine Learning
abstract:
The ten things that actually go wrong. Most ML projects do not fail because
someone chose the wrong algorithm — they fail on data collection, data
quality, representativeness, features, or the engineering around the model.
This document walks all ten challenges from the notes: data collection,
insufficient data, non-representative data, poor quality data, insufficient
features, overfitting, underfitting, software integration, deployment, and
cost — with the diagnosis, the mathematics where it exists, the visual
signature of each, and the concrete fix.

blocks.t: The Ten Challenges
The pattern in the list

Challenges 1–5 are about data. Challenges 6–7 are about
the model. Challenges 8–10 are about engineering and
economics. Only two of the ten are what most beginners think ML is about.
That ratio is the single most useful thing on this page.
Challenge 1 — Data Collection

Before anything else, you must have the data. The notes list the sources
(Topic 10 covers this in full): CSV/Excel files, JSON, SQL databases, APIs, and
web scraping.

items:
The business wants to predict something nobody has ever
 recorded. You are not building a model, you are building a logging pipeline
 and waiting six months.

Customer data in Salesforce, transactions in Postgres,
 clicks in a warehouse, support tickets in Zendesk. The join key is inconsistent
 or absent.

GDPR, DPDP, HIPAA. Some data cannot be moved
 across borders, and some cannot be used for the purpose you want.

Use it only when no API exists. It breaks
 when the page layout changes and may violate terms of service.

blocks.t: The question to ask in the first meeting

"Where does this data come from today, who owns it, and how far back does it
go?" If nobody can answer, the project timeline is not eight weeks.
Challenge 2 — Insufficient Data / Labelled Data

ML is statistics; statistics needs sample size. With too few rows the model
cannot distinguish signal from noise, and the gap between training and
validation performance stays wide.

blocks.cap:
Left: a non-representative sample (Challenge 3). Right: the learning
 curve for Challenge 2 — the shaded gap between training and validation
 accuracy is overfitting, and it narrows as rows are added.

blocks.t: Labelled data is the real bottleneck

Raw data is cheap; labels are expensive. A radiologist annotating scans
or a lawyer tagging clauses costs real money per row. This is why
semi-supervised learning, active learning, weak supervision and transfer
learning exist — all four are answers to "we cannot afford more labels".
What to do about it

items:
Plot a learning curve before asking for more data. If validation
 accuracy has already plateaued, more rows will not help — your
 problem is Challenge 5 (features) or 7 (underfitting).

Transfer learning. Start from a model trained on a large related
 dataset and fine-tune. Standard practice in vision and NLP.

Data augmentation. Flip, crop, rotate images; paraphrase or
 back-translate text; SMOTE for tabular minority classes (Topic 80).

Simpler model. With 200 rows, use logistic regression, not a
 neural network. Fewer parameters need less data to estimate.

Active learning. Label the points the model is least certain
 about; you get far more value per labelled row.

blocks.t: Challenge 3 — Non-Representative Data
The definition

Your training data does not look like the data the model will actually meet in
production. The model is not wrong about its world — it is that its
world is not the real one.

This is sampling bias, and it is the most dangerous item on this list
because the model's offline metrics look excellent. The gap only appears after
deployment.
Why the metrics lie

The i.i.d. assumption underlying supervised learning is that train and
deployment data are drawn from the same distribution:
$P_{\text{train}}(X,Y)=P_{\text{deploy}}(X,Y)$. Your test set is drawn from
$P_{\text{train}}$, so a biased sample produces a test set biased in
exactly the same way. The test set cannot detect the flaw, because it
shares it.

head: Classic example
What went wrong
rows: 1936 Literary Digest poll predicted Landon over Roosevelt
2.4 million responses, but sampled from telephone and car-registration lists — wealthy households in the Depression
Face recognition failing on darker skin
Training sets dominated by light-skinned faces
A hiring model that penalised women
Trained on ten years of a company's own biased hiring decisions
Loan default model trained only on approved loans
The rejected applicants — the informative cases — are absent by construction

blocks.t: Survivorship bias

The loan example is worth dwelling on. You only observe outcomes for applicants
you approved. The model learns "who defaults among people we already
thought were safe", not "who defaults". Abraham Wald's WWII aircraft
analysis is the same error: armour the parts with no bullet holes, because the
planes hit there never came back.
What to do about it

Audit the sampling mechanism, not the sample. Compare the feature distributions
of your training set against known population statistics. Use stratified
sampling. For deployed systems, monitor the input distribution continuously
(population stability index) so you are alerted when production data drifts away
from training data.
Challenge 4 — Poor Quality Data

blocks.cap:
Three distinct quality problems, each with a different remedy.
 Left: three outliers rotate the entire regression line. Middle: missingness
 concentrated in specific columns. Right: label noise, which caps achievable
 accuracy no matter what you do.

head: Problem
Effect
Fix (topic)
rows: Most algorithms refuse to run; naive filling distorts the distribution
Squared-error and weight-based models are dragged badly
Leakage between train and test; inflated metrics
Dates as strings, numbers as objects
Re-annotate, use consensus labels, robust losses

blocks.t: The industry cliché is true

Data scientists report spending 60–80% of their time on data cleaning. The
notes' emphasis on Feature Engineering (Part II of this course — 22 of the 82
topics) reflects exactly this reality.
Challenge 5 — Insufficient Features
The ceiling nobody can lift

If the information needed to predict $y$ is not present in $X$, no
algorithm can recover it. This is not a modelling problem and it cannot be
fixed by hyperparameter tuning.

blocks.cap:
The same 250 students. With CGPA alone the two classes overlap
 completely and the Bayes-optimal accuracy is poor. Add the feature that
 actually drives the outcome and a straight line separates them perfectly.

blocks.t: The Bayes error

For any feature set $X$, the lowest achievable error of any classifier is
the Bayes error
R^{*} = \mathbb{E}_X \left[1-\max_c P(Y=c \mid X)\right].

Because $R^*$ is a property of the joint distribution, changing the algorithm
cannot reduce it. Only changing $X$ — adding a feature that carries genuine
information about $Y$ — lowers the floor. This is the mathematical statement
of "better features beat better algorithms".

The remedies are the whole of Feature Engineering: feature construction
(Topic 31) to build informative columns from domain knowledge, and
feature extraction (Topics 32–33) when you have too many rather than too
few.
Challenges 6 & 7 — Overfitting and Underfitting

blocks.cap:
The same 26 points fitted with polynomial degrees 1, 4 and 17.
 Degree 1 cannot represent the curve at all. Degree 17 passes through nearly
 every training point — and would be wildly wrong on a new one.

head: Overfitting
Underfitting
rows: Model is too complex; "har point pe vishwas"
Model is too simple; "pattern dikha hi nahi"
Too many parameters, too few rows, noise memorised, leakage
Model too rigid, too few features, over-regularised, under-trained
More data, regularisation (L1/L2, Topics 41–43), simpler model, dropout, early stopping, bagging, cross-validation
More complex model, more/better features, less regularisation, train longer, boosting

blocks.t: The three ways to reach the sweet spot

The notes name them explicitly, and each has its own topic later:
Regularisation (41–43), Bagging (60–61), and
Boosting (65–69). Regularisation constrains a single model; bagging
averages many high-variance models down; boosting composes many high-bias models
up.
Data leakage — overfitting's invisible cause

The nastiest form of overfitting is not model complexity, it is leakage:
information from the test set contaminating training. Classic instances:

items:
Scaling or imputing before the train/test split, so test statistics
 leak into training.

A feature computed using future information ("total purchases this year"
 when predicting a purchase in March).
Duplicate rows spread across both splits.

Oversampling before splitting, so copies of the same minority row appear
 in both.

blocks.t:
The symptom is a suspiciously perfect validation score followed by a
catastrophic production score. Fit every transformer on train only —
this is the whole reason Pipelines (Topic 17) exist.
Challenge 8 — Software Integration

A model that lives in a notebook produces no business value. The integration
problems are real engineering problems:

items:
Training/serving skew. The transformation applied in production
 differs from the one applied at training. Overwhelmingly the most common
 production bug in ML.

Latency budgets. The business allows 50 ms end-to-end; your
 feature computation takes 400 ms.

Version compatibility. A model pickled under scikit-learn 1.3
 will not reliably load under 1.6.

Language mismatch. The model is Python; the application is Java
 or Go. Hence ONNX, PMML, and REST/gRPC microservices.

Feature availability. A feature that exists in your historical
 warehouse may not exist at request time.

blocks.t: The fix has a name

Pipelines (Topic 17) and feature stores. If the same serialised pipeline
object does both the training transform and the serving transform, skew is
structurally impossible.
Challenge 9 — Deployment and Offline Learning

This is Topic 03 restated as a risk. A batch-trained model is a frozen artefact:
it does not know the world has changed. Deployment brings its own failures —
model rot from concept drift, no rollback path, no monitoring of live
performance, and delayed labels (you may not learn whether a loan defaulted for
two years).
Challenge 10 — Cost Involved

head: Cost centre
What it actually is
rows: Purchasing datasets, paying annotators, building collection infrastructure
GPU hours for training; the far larger recurring bill for inference at scale
Raw data, features, model versions, logs — retained for audit
The scarcest and most expensive input
Retraining, monitoring, on-call — typically exceeding the original build cost
Six months on a model that a SQL query and three business rules would have matched

blocks.t: Always establish a baseline first

Before training anything, measure a trivial baseline: predict the mean, predict
the majority class, or apply the existing hand-written business rule. If your
model beats it by 1%, the project may not be worth its lifetime cost. This
single habit prevents more wasted effort than any modelling technique.
Code: Diagnosing Which Challenge You Have

import numpy as np, pandas as pd
from sklearn.model_selection import learning_curve, train_test_split
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.dummy import DummyClassifier
from sklearn.metrics import accuracy_score

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
X = rng.normal(0, 1, (1200, 12))
y = (X[:, 0] + 0.7 * X[:, 1] + rng.normal(0, .8, 1200) > 0).astype(int)
Xtr, Xte, ytr, yte = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=.25, random_state=0)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------
# STEP 0 -- CHALLENGE 10: what does doing nothing get you?
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------
base = DummyClassifier(strategy="most_frequent").fit(Xtr, ytr)
print("baseline (majority class):", base.score(Xte, yte))
# Every number below must be compared against THIS, not against zero.

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------
# STEP 1 -- CHALLENGES 6 & 7: overfitting or underfitting?
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------
model = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=200, random_state=0).fit(Xtr, ytr)
tr = accuracy_score(ytr, model.predict(Xtr))
te = accuracy_score(yte, model.predict(Xte))
gap = tr - te
print(f"train {tr:.3f}  test {te:.3f}  gap {gap:.3f}")

if gap > 0.10:
    print("-> OVERFITTING: regularise, simplify, or get more data")
elif tr < 0.75:
    print("-> UNDERFITTING: more capacity or better features")
else:
    print("-> reasonable fit")

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------
# STEP 2 -- CHALLENGE 2: will more DATA help? read the learning curve.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------
sizes, tr_sc, va_sc = learning_curve(
    LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000), X, y,
    train_sizes=np.linspace(.1, 1.0, 8), cv=5, scoring="accuracy")

improvement = va_sc.mean(axis=1)[-1] - va_sc.mean(axis=1)[-3]
print(f"validation gain over the last 25% of data: {improvement:+.4f}")
if improvement < 0.005:
    print("-> validation has PLATEAUED: more rows will NOT help.")
    print("   Your bottleneck is FEATURES (challenge 5), not data (challenge 2).")

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------
# STEP 3 -- CHALLENGE 4: audit data quality before anything else
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------
df = pd.DataFrame(X).assign(target=y)
report = pd.DataFrame({
    "missing_pct":  df.isna().mean(),
    "n_unique":     df.nunique(),
    "dtype":        df.dtypes.astype(str),
})
print(report.head())
print("duplicate rows:", df.duplicated().sum())   # drop these BEFORE splitting

# outliers per column, IQR rule
q1, q3 = df.quantile(.25), df.quantile(.75)
iqr = q3 - q1
outliers = ((df < q1 - 1.5 * iqr) | (df > q3 + 1.5 * iqr)).sum()
print("outliers per column:\n", outliers[outliers > 0])

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------
# STEP 4 -- CHALLENGE 3: is train distributed like production?
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------
def psi(expected, actual, bins=10):
    """Population Stability Index. >0.25 => the distribution has shifted."""
    cuts = np.percentile(expected, np.linspace(0, 100, bins + 1))
    cuts[0], cuts[-1] = -np.inf, np.inf
    e = np.histogram(expected, cuts)[0] / len(expected) + 1e-6
    a = np.histogram(actual,   cuts)[0] / len(actual)   + 1e-6
    return float(((a - e) * np.log(a / e)).sum())

production = rng.normal(0.4, 1.2, 2000)          # drifted feature
print("PSI:", round(psi(Xtr[:, 0], production), 3),
      "-> non-representative" if psi(Xtr[:, 0], production) > .25 else "-> stable")

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------
# STEP 5 -- CHALLENGE 8: the leakage-proof way to transform
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer

# WRONG -- scaler sees test statistics, metrics become optimistic
# X_all = StandardScaler().fit_transform(X); then split

# RIGHT -- one object, fit on train only, reused verbatim in production
pipe = make_pipeline(SimpleImputer(strategy="median"),
                     StandardScaler(),
                     LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000)).fit(Xtr, ytr)
print("leak-free test score:", pipe.score(Xte, yte))
# joblib.dump(pipe, "model.pkl")  -> serving applies the IDENTICAL transform
Summary
Everything on one page

items:
1. Data collection — it may not exist, may be scattered, may be
 legally restricted. Scrape only when there is no API.

2. Insufficient data — especially labelled data. Read the
 learning curve before demanding more rows.

3. Non-representative data — sampling bias. The most dangerous
 item, because your test set shares the flaw and cannot detect it.

4. Poor quality data — missing values, outliers, duplicates,
 wrong dtypes, label noise. This is what Part II of the course is for.

5. Insufficient features — a hard ceiling set by the Bayes error.
 No algorithm can beat it; only new information can.
6. Overfitting — low bias, high variance. Big train–test gap.
7. Underfitting — high bias, low variance. Both errors high.

8. Software integration — training/serving skew, latency,
 versioning. Pipelines are the structural fix.
9. Deployment — frozen models rot under concept drift.

10. Cost — compute, people, and above all maintenance. Always
 measure a trivial baseline first.

blocks.t: Questions you will actually be asked

Q. Your model scores 0.94 in validation and 0.61 in production. What are
your hypotheses, in order?

(1) Data leakage — a transformer fitted before the split, or a feature using
future information. (2) Non-representative training data — the test set shares
the sampling bias so it could not catch it. (3) Concept drift between training
and deployment. (4) Training/serving skew — production applies a different
transformation. Check leakage first; it is both the most common and the
cheapest to verify.
Q. Training accuracy 0.99, validation accuracy 0.71. What now?

Textbook overfitting. In order of cost: more data; stronger regularisation
(raise $\lambda$, lower max_depth); a simpler model; feature selection;
bagging. And check for leakage — a 28-point gap is large enough to be
suspicious.
Q. Both training and validation accuracy are 0.62. More data?

No. Equal, poor scores mean underfitting — the model cannot represent the
pattern it already has. More rows of the same information change nothing. Add
capacity or, more likely, add features.

Q. How do you detect non-representative training data before
deploying?

You cannot detect it from the test set — it is drawn from the same biased
distribution. You must compare against external ground truth: known population
statistics, a deliberately randomised holdout, or the input distribution of live
traffic (PSI monitoring).
Q. Which challenge causes the most project failures?

Data problems, 3 through 5. Choosing between XGBoost and a random forest moves
accuracy by a point or two; a biased sample or a missing feature decides whether
the project works at all.
